report:
## Evidence on Chlorhexidine-Alcohol vs. Iodine-Alcohol for Cesarean SSI Prevention

The evidence is **genuinely mixed**, so your skepticism has some basis—but the claim is not clearly false either.

**Supporting the claim:** The largest trial directly comparing the two *alcohol-based* preparations—a single-center RCT of 1,147 women (Tuuli et al., NEJM 2016)—found SSI rates of 4.0% (chlorhexidine-alcohol) vs. 7.3% (iodine-alcohol), RR 0.55 (95% CI 0.34–0.90, P=0.02). A 2018 meta-analysis and a Cochrane review (2020, moderate-certainty evidence) also concluded chlorhexidine is probably slightly superior to povidone-iodine for cesarean SSI prevention.

**Contradicting the claim:** The CAPICA trial (Springel et al., 2017, n≈1,400) found **no significant difference** in SSI (4.5% vs. 4.6%) when comparing chlorhexidine-alcohol to povidone-iodine—though it used *aqueous* iodine, not iodine-alcohol. A 2025 trial-sequential meta-analysis concluded that pooled high-quality RCTs showed **no benefit** of alcoholic chlorhexidine. A 2024 network meta-analysis found no significant difference between chlorhexidine-alcohol and iodine-alcohol for abdominal surgeries (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.94–1.54), though it ranked alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine as most likely effective.

**Bottom line:** The claim rests heavily on one positive single-center trial. Subsequent multicenter trials and newer meta-analyses have failed to replicate the benefit, and the overall evidence is inconsistent rather than definitively supporting superiority. Your view that the claim may be overstated is reasonable, but calling it outright "false" goes beyond what the conflicting evidence supports.

**Sources:**

- https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28599898/
- https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2025.1641815/full
- https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32580252/
